facts.statement: The genus Leptostyrax was described by Williston in 1900.
The type species of the genus Leptostyrax is Leptostyrax macrorhiza.
Leptostyrax stychi is a valid species within the genus, described by Schmitz, Thies, and Kriwet in 2010.
Leptostyrax fossils have been found in North America, Europe, Africa, and Australia.
facts.quote: It contains two valid species, L. macrorhiza and L. stychi, found in North America, Europe, Africa, and Australia.

facts.statement: Leptostyrax is considered one of the earliest known lamniform sharks that underwent an adaptive radiation in the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: It is among the earliest known lamniforms which underwent an adaptive radiation in the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Vertebrae tentatively assigned to Leptostyrax macrorhiza suggest the shark reached lengths of 6.3 to 8.3 meters, potentially making it one of the largest Cretaceous sharks.
facts.quote: However, vertebrae tentatively assigned to L. macrorhiza suggest lengths of 6.3 - 8.3 m, making it potentially one of the largest Cretaceous sharks.

facts.statement: The tearing type dentition of Leptostyrax suggests it preferred moderately large prey such as bony fishes.
facts.quote: This tearing type dentition suggests Leptostyrax preferred moderately large prey like bony fishes.

facts.statement: Leptostyrax belongs to the parent group Eoptolamnidae.
The family of Leptostyrax is Eoptolamnidae.
Leptostyrax is classified in the class Chondrichthyes.
Leptostyrax lived from the Barremian to the Bartonian stages, between 125.77 and 37.71 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Bartonian (125.77 to 37.71 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Leptostyrax possessed teeth similar to the modern sand tiger shark, featuring a tall, narrow primary cusp and smaller secondary lateral cusps.
rejected.quote: Leptostyrax had teeth similar to the modern sand tiger shark in having a tall, narrow primary cusp, and smaller secondary lateral cusps.
